sentences.text: The body of this fish was protected by thick ganoid scales.
Its lower jaw featured slender, single-cusped or two-cusped marginal teeth, while smaller interior teeth formed dense batteries on the skull.
A complete fossil from the Toarcian of Hungary represents the only known specimen from eastern Europe.
Reports of this fish in India are considered erroneous.
An indeterminate species is known from the Moltrasio Formation in Italy.
William Elford Leach named the genus in 1822 based on Early Jurassic remains found in Lyme Regis, Dorset, England.
The animal was relatively rare during the Triassic but underwent a large burst in diversification after the Triassic-Jurassic extinction event.
Scientists suggest it survived the extinction because it was a heavily-scaled generalist, unlike most Triassic dapediids which had specialized feeding or less armor.
Adaptations may have helped it survive the Toarcian Oceanic Anoxic Event, though its abundance declined dramatically around that time and it went extinct shortly after.
It is thought to have been a durophagous predator that used slender marginal teeth to grasp prey and smaller interior teeth to crush hard-shelled organisms.
Evidence suggests it likely engaged in scavenging, as one specimen was found inside the body cavity of the ammonite Lytoceras, where it likely became stuck while trying to scavenge.
Dapedius is a synonym for the genus, which belongs to the extinct order Semionotiformes and the extinct family Dapediidae.
This fish lived from the Late Triassic to the Middle Jurassic, spanning the late Norian to early Aalenian, and was one of the most abundant fossil fish in Early Jurassic European deposits.
It inhabited the western Tethys Ocean surrounding Europe, with fossils found in Italy, the UK, France, Germany, and Hungary.
The monophyly of the genus is debated, with some studies suggesting it is probably paraphyletic.
